statement: Lecture 8 agenda: approaching distributed systems, designing a load balancer, remote and distributed locks, synchronizing consumers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda: - Approaching distributed systems - Designing Load Balancer - Remote and Distributed locks - Synchronizing Consumers

statement: A distributed system is multiple components on multiple machines that together act as a single coherent system solving a bigger problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Multiple Components Multiple Machines } Single coherent system ↓ Solves a bigger problem

statement: The best and the worst thing about distributed systems: anything that could go wrong would go wrong.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The best and the worst thing about distributed systems is Anything that could go wrong would go wrong

statement: Key to designing a good distributed system: start with a Day0 architecture, scale each component, see how it performs under load, rectify the system, re-architect, and repeat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Start with a Day0 architecture and scale each component ↓ see how it performs under load rectify the system re-architect and repeat

statement: Reasons for distributed systems: scale, horizontal scalability and fault tolerance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why distributed systems ? - Scale - Horizontal Scalability - Fault Tolerance

statement: The load balancer is one of the most important components in any system, and we kind of take it for granted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One of the most important component in any system - load Ba[cut off] * We kind of take it for granted

statement: Advantages of using a load balancer: fault tolerance and no over-clocked (overloaded) server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Advantages of using a load Balancer - Fault tolerance - No over-clocked server

statement: A load balancing algorithm decides which backend server to choose for a request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Load Balancing Algorithms * which backend server to choose *

statement: Round robin: for uniform infrastructure, distribute the load iteratively (requests 1,4 / 2,5 / 3,6 across three servers).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Round Robin Uniform infrastructure Distribute the load iteratively

statement: Weighted round robin: for non-uniform infrastructure, distribute the load iteratively but as per weights; the bigger machine gets more requests.
topic: load balancer > algorithms > weighted round robin
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Weighted Round Robin Non- Uniform infrastructure Distribute the load iteratively but as per weights

statement: Least connections: pick the server having the least connections from the load balancer; use it when response times have a big variance (e.g. analytics).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: least Connections Pick the server having the least connections from the load balancer When response times has a big variance * Analytics

statement: Design requirements for the load balancer: balance the load, tunable algorithm, scaling beyond one machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements : - balance the load - tunable algorithm - scaling beyond one machine

statement: Terminology: the LB server (the machine running the load balancer) versus backend servers (the servers it forwards to).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Terminology : LB Server , Backend Server

statement: Brainstorm agenda for the LB design: LB configurations, monitoring, availability, extensibility.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Brainstorm : LB configurations , Monitoring , Availability, Extensibility

statement: Example setup: LB server at 10.0.0.1 holding a list of backend servers 10.0.0.7, 10.0.0.8, 10.0.0.9, all on port 8081.
speaker: teacher

statement: For each client request the LB holds two TCP connections, client to LB (TCP1) and LB to backend (TCP2), and keeps a map tcp1 → tcp2 to forward data both ways; a second client gets tcp3 → tcp4.
detail: Diagram D-03; the LB is drawn as 10.0.0.1 :9000.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: { tcp1 → tcp2 tcp3 → tcp4 }

statement: The teacher's experimental load balancer ARLB is a super simple reverse proxy (load balancer) in Go, repo github.com/arpitbhayani/arlb.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ARLB - Experimental Reverse Proxy and Load Balancer Super simple, experimental reverse proxy (load balancer) in Golang.

statement: In lb.go a Backend has Host, Port, IsHealthy and NumRequests; InitLB hardcodes four localhost backends on ports 8081-8084 and a hashed balancing strategy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: type Backend struct { Host string Port int IsHealthy bool NumRequests int }

statement: The LB listens for TCP on port 9090 and, for every accepted connection, runs proxy() in a goroutine with a new UUID request id.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: net.Listen("tcp", ":9090") ... go lb.proxy(IncomingReq{ srcConn: connection, reqId: uuid.NewString(), })

statement: proxy() picks a backend via strategy.GetNextBackend, dials it over TCP (writing "backend not available" to the client on failure), increments NumRequests and copies bytes both ways with two io.Copy goroutines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: backend := lb.strategy.GetNextBackend(req) ... go io.Copy(backendConn, req.srcConn) go io.Copy(req.srcConn, backendConn)

statement: strategy.go defines a strategy interface (GetNextBackend, RegisterBackend, PrintTopology) with round-robin, static and hashed implementations; round robin is Index = (Index + 1) % len(Backends).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: s.Index = (s.Index + 1) % len(s.Backends) return s.Backends[s.Index]

statement: The hashed strategy hashes backends and request ids (md5 byte sum mod 19) onto sorted occupied slots and picks the next slot (consistent-hashing style).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: slot := hash(req.reqId) index := sort.Search(...) return s.Backends[index%len(s.Backends)]

statement: The LB's run loop listens on an events channel to handle exit, backend add and strategy change at runtime.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: case CMD_Exit: ... case CMD_BackendAdd: ... case CMD_StrategyChange:

statement: LB configuration: the list of backend servers (ip:port), the balancing algorithm and the health endpoint.
detail: Second key written `balancy` (cramped); audio context is the balancing algorithm.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: { b.servs: [ ip: pr. ], balancy: algo: health_endpoint: " " }

statement: The LB configuration is stored in a DB and the LB server keeps an in-memory copy synced from it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DB ... syn-

statement: An orchestrator (several instances) sends heartbeats to the backend servers on their health endpoint (/health on port 8081) and updates their health in the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Orchestrator hb /status /health 8081

statement: If the LB polls the DB every 10 seconds, for up to one polling interval it can keep sending requests to a backend that is already dead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 10sec 1 poll

statement: Developers change the LB configuration through an LB Console API that writes to the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: LB Console API Dev

statement: The LB server exposes a separate meta/admin port (9091) next to its data port (9090).
speaker: teacher

statement: Instead of polling, config changes in the DB are pushed to the LB servers through CDC into a pub/sub pipe.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDC

statement: The orchestrator also monitors the LB servers themselves.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Orchestrator ... LB

statement: Vitals of LB and backend servers go to a central metrics store (Prometheus) for monitoring; the orchestrator reads utilisation from it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Metric Vitals Prometheus monitrng

statement: Clients reach multiple LB servers through DNS: one domain name resolves to all LB server IPs (10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2, ...).
speaker: teacher

statement: A private CoreDNS resolves the LB's domain name (e.g. payments.lb.google.com) to the LB server IPs; the orchestrator updates the DNS entries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CoreDNS paym.lb. googl.com → 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2

statement: Recommended reading: the φ-accrual failure detection algorithm.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read about φ-accrual failure detection algorithm

statement: Orchestrator's focused responsibilities: watch backend health, update the DB when a backend is unhealthy (changes reach LB servers through pub/sub), and monitor and scale LB servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: keeps an eye on the health of the backend servers ... orchestrator updates the DB ... Monitors health of LB servers

statement: The orchestrator decides LB scaling on CPU, memory and number of TCP connections, using data from the monitoring component (Prometheus).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Scaling will happen on CPU, Mem, # TCP connections where do we have this data ? Monitoring Component ↳ Prometheus !!

statement: Final LB design: users resolve lb.payments.google.com via private Core DNS and connect to the LB servers, which forward to backend servers; config flows from LB Console APIs to the DB and via CDC and Redis pub/sub to the LB servers; an orchestrator (leader election) heartbeats LB and backend servers, updates the DB and DNS and queries Prometheus; autoscaling acts on metrics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Core DNS private infra lb.payments.google.com LB Servers Redis as PubSub CDC Orchestrator leaderElec prometheus Autoscaling LB Console APIs

statement: Recommended paper: Maglev, a fast and reliable software load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read this paper : Maglev : A fast and reliable software load balancer

statement: Remote locks are locks managed by a central machine, the lock manager; the machines coordinate through it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Remote locks: Locks managed by a central machine ↓ Lock Manager ... The 3 machines co-ordinate through a central lock manager

statement: Threads synchronize through mutex and semaphore, processes through disk, machines through a remote lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Multiple threads synchronize through Mutex & Semaphore Multiple processes synchronize through Disk Multiple machines synchronize through Remote lock

statement: Process-level example: "apt-get upgrade" cannot be run twice concurrently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Interesting example: "apt-get upgrade" cannot be run twice concurrently

statement: Running example: synchronize multiple consumers over an unprotected remote queue so only one consumer calls the queue at a time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: lets synchronize multiple consumers over an unprotected remote queue ... We want one consumer to make call to the queue at a time

statement: Lock brainstorm: store which consumer holds a queue's lock in a database (queue7 → C1) with a TTL; the store needs key-value, atomic operations and TTL; Redlock is named.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: queue7 → C1 TTL k,v Atomic TTL Redlock

statement: Consumer's pseudocode: ACQ_LOCK(), READ_MSG(), REL_LOCK(); all consumers wait on ACQ_LOCK() while one of them does READ_MSG().
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ACQ_LOCK() READ_MSG() REL_LOCK() All consumers wait on ACQ_LOCK() while one of them READ_MSG()

statement: Requirements from the lock manager: atomic operations so two machines do not both acquire the lock, and automatic expiration to avoid perpetual locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: - Atomic Operations → so that two machines do not ACQ_LOCK() - Automatic Expiration → avoid perpetual locking

statement: Redis and DynamoDB are choices for the lock store; Redis is popular because it is in-memory (fast).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, which DB ? Redis , DynamoDB ↑ Popular choice because in-mem (fast)

statement: Implementation: set a key in Redis saying which consumer holds the lock, e.g. queue7 : consumer 2 with expiry 300 s (5 min).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: eg: queue7 : consumer 2 [ex : 300] lock held by consumer 2 expiration : 5 min

statement: acquire_lock(q): loop forever calling redis.setnx(q, consumer_id, ex=300); return if it returns 1, otherwise continue.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: While True: v = redis.setnx (q , consumer_id , ex = 300) if v == 1 : return else : continue

statement: release_lock(q): get the key and delete it only if its value equals my consumer_id; the get-compare-delete is executed atomically with a Lua script via EVAL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: v = redis.get (q) if v == consumer_id : redis.delete (q) "EVAL" Executed atomically using LUA script

statement: Redis as a central lock manager: every consumer talks to one Redis instance for the lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis lock Manager

statement: MongoDB transactions use remote locks on the involved rows.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MongoDB transaction uses remote locks on involved rows

statement: Distributed locks with Redis are called Redlock: take the remote lock and distribute it over 5 independent Redis master nodes with no replication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Distributed locks [Redlock] ← Distributed locks with Redis Idea: What we did in remote lock, just distribute it 5 master nodes of Redis

statement: Redlock acquire: the client goes through the 5 nodes trying ACQ_LOCK with a timeout; if acquired on more than 50% it is ACQUIRED, else it releases the lock on acquired instances and returns FAILED.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: client goes through 5 nodes , trying to ACQ_LOCK - if lock acquired on > 50% then ACQUIRED - else ... return FAILED

statement: Why Redlock: with distributed locking there is no single point of failure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But why are we doing this? With distributed locking we now do not have a SPoF

statement: Further reading: Chubby paper (lock service for loosely coupled distributed systems), arpitbhayani.me/blogs (>13 posts on distributed systems), Martin Kleppmann on Redlock and its GitHub implementation, and the AsliEngineering video on distributed transactions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Chubby : lock service for loosely coupled distributed systems ... REDLOCK . Martin Kleppmann and implementation on GitHub
